## TL;DR

The Android Hub back gesture was a no-op on tailnet discovery because the shell keeps `picker`, `settings`, `add` and `discover` as local Vue routes, while Capacitor's App plugin only falls back to WebView history when no `backButton` listener exists. The shell never creates history entries, so there was nothing to pop. I added a small, pure back-navigation state machine (`mobile/src/back-navigation.ts`), wired it to Capacitor's `backButton` event on Android only, and covered the mapping plus listener lifecycle with 18 focused tests. Discovery returns to the picker regardless of whether it is signed out, loading, empty or errored. Settings and Add return to the picker; an open edit sheet closes first; a visible device-lock gate ignores the gesture; only the picker root exits the app. The scoped `repoos check` passed. I did not run the app on a physical Android device, so real-gesture verification remains unobserved.

## Work and rationale

The first step was tracing how Android back is delivered. The native App plugin installs an `OnBackPressedCallback`. Its handler checks whether JavaScript has registered a `backButton` listener. If one exists, it notifies JavaScript and consumes the event. If none exists, it only calls `webView.goBack()` when the WebView can go back. The Hub shell's screens are not WebView history entries; they are a single `route` ref in `mobile/src/App.vue`. Consequently, at discovery `canGoBack()` was false and the gesture did nothing. That explains why the on-screen Servers button worked while the system gesture did not.

The fix needed explicit navigation, not a history shim. I created `mobile/src/back-navigation.ts` with a narrow model:

- `HubBackState` holds the current route, whether the edit-server sheet is open, and whether the device-lock gate is showing.
- `hubBackAction` applies priorities: lock gate ignores the gesture, then an open sheet closes, then any non-picker route shows the picker, and only the picker root exits.
- `runHubBack` invokes exactly one corresponding handler and returns the action, which makes tests assert both `HubBackAction` and callback effects.
- `installHubBackButton` gates registration to Android, subscribes through an injected function, and returns an idempotent teardown.

`App.vue` now imports `App` from `@capacitor/app` and calls `installHubBackButton` in `onMounted`, passing `App.addListener("backButton", listener)` as the subscription. The state getter reads live refs, so the handler always sees the current screen. Handlers reuse the existing `closeSheet` and `backToPicker` functions; exit calls `App.exitApp()`. Teardown runs in `onUnmounted`, and a guard disposes immediately if the component unmounts before listener registration resolves.

Two ordering decisions matter. First, registration happens before loading persisted state and the discovery request so the listener is available during startup. Second, the lock gate is checked before the sheet and route. The gate is modal and security-sensitive: allowing back to close it, navigate away, or exit the app would be surprising and could weaken the intent of the device-lock feature. Ignoring the gesture while it is visible is the conservative choice.

Discovery content deliberately does not influence navigation. Signed-out, loading, empty, and error states all set `route = "discover"`; the back decision only needs that route. This avoids coupling the shell navigator to the discovery response shape and prevents a future message/error branch from accidentally disabling back. The tests still name those states explicitly so the acceptance criterion is visible in the suite.

The picker root exits the app. Capacitor's plugin consumes the gesture once a listener exists, so without an explicit exit the root would become a dead back button. Exiting at the root preserves normal Android behavior, while all sub-screens return to the picker. iOS and the web dev build never subscribe; their platform-native behavior is unchanged. This also keeps the browser preview useful, where a synthetic Capacitor back event would not occur.

I updated `docs/mobile-architecture.md` with a short "System back navigation (Android)" section so future native-shell work does not assume WebView history exists.

## Approaches tried

I considered relying on WebView history: call `history.pushState` when entering settings, add and discovery, then let Capacitor's default `webView.goBack()` pop them. That would reduce custom code, but it mixes visual routes with browser history and requires careful handling of sheets, the lock gate, and startup fixtures. It also depends on a plugin fallback that is easy to change. The explicit state machine is easier to test and explains intent directly.

I also considered an Android-native `OnBackPressedCallback` in `MainActivity.java`. That would work, but the bridge between native code and the Vue route would be larger, harder to unit-test here, and would duplicate logic for the lock and sheet. The App plugin is already a dependency and exposes exactly the event needed.

For testability I avoided importing `@capacitor/app` in the new module. The module receives a subscription function instead. Tests drive fake listeners and assert handler calls without Capacitor native mocks or an Android build, so they run in the normal gate.

## Challenges and blockers

The first scoped check failed on TypeScript, not behavior. I typed the test helper as an intersection of `HubBackHandlers` and `ReturnType<typeof vi.fn>`, and Vitest's generic mock type was not assignable to a `() => void` signature. The fix was to let inference produce `vi.fn<() => void>()` mocks and drop the explicit intersection. Both the UI typecheck/build and the focused tests then passed.

There is no installed Android SDK, emulator or device in this runner, and the task explicitly warns against claiming real-device verification. I verified the TypeScript mobile app build (`bun run build` in `mobile/`), the focused test file, and the full scoped gate, but I did not observe the gesture on hardware. The native App plugin behavior is based on its Android source and the Capacitor contract; a reviewer with the phone should confirm the gesture visibly.

The worktree is behind main, which has newer bookkeeping for other tasks. The branch diff versus main includes stale activity lines in sibling task files; RepoOS's handoff/close-out integration handles those from current main. I did not edit or commit other tasks' files, and all implementation changes are limited to the mobile shell, the focused test, and the architecture doc.

## Key learnings

- Capacitor's App plugin changes the default back behavior as soon as JavaScript attaches a `backButton` listener. A shell that uses local routes must handle every route explicitly, including the root exit, or back becomes dead.
- Navigation state is easiest to reason about when it is pure and ordered. Putting the lock gate first, then sheets, then routes, gives one deterministic answer per gesture and is simple to test exhaustively.
- The Hub's discovery screen has several content states but one navigation identity. Keeping back decisions independent of message/error state is both simpler and more robust than branching on response details.
- Test-only seams such as an injected subscription function can verify native event wiring without making the production module import a native plugin, which keeps the normal repo test gate fast and independent of the mobile toolchain.
